section.title: Boasting About Tomorrow
section.sectionRationale: James turns from worldliness in general to one of its most respectable forms: confident planning that leaves God out. He addresses the traveling merchant who maps out a year of profit as if tomorrow were his to command, exposes the arrogance of such self-assured boasting, and calls for a life lived under the Lord's will. He closes with a sharp reminder that knowing the good and not doing it is itself sin.
section.thesis: To plan our lives as though the future were ours is arrogant boasting, for life is a vanishing mist; humble living says, if the Lord wills, and refuses the sin of knowing the right and failing to do it.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the presumptuous planner rebuked and taught to say if the Lord wills; and the closing principle that knowing good and not doing it is sin.

verses.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, {{emporeuomai|carry on business}}, and make a profit.”
You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a {{atmis|mist}} that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.”
As it is, you boast in your {{alazoneia|proud intentions}}. All such boasting is evil.
Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.

emporeuomai.gloss: To travel for trade, to carry on business, the root of the word emporium. James pictures the confident merchant planning a year of buying and selling to turn a profit. The problem is not commerce itself but the godless self-assurance with which the plan is made.

atmis.gloss: A vapor or mist, a puff of steam that appears briefly and is gone. James uses it for the brevity and fragility of human life, echoing the vapor of Ecclesiastes and the fleeting breath of the Psalms. The image demolishes the illusion that we command our own tomorrows.

alazoneia.gloss: Boasting, arrogance, pretentious self-confidence. It names the proud presumption of planning as though the future were ours to guarantee. James calls all such boasting evil, for it usurps a sovereignty that belongs to God alone, who holds every tomorrow in His hand.

basic.context: James takes on the successful planner. Picture a merchant saying, tomorrow we will go to that city, spend a year, do business, and make a profit. Sounds sensible. But James says, you do not even know what tomorrow holds. Your life is a mist, here for a moment and gone. The arrogance is not in planning but in planning as if you were in charge of the future. Instead, he says, live saying, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that. To leave God out and boast in your own plans is evil. And he ends with a jab that applies to everyone: if you know the right thing to do and do not do it, that is sin.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prescriptive wisdom, correcting an attitude rather than forbidding an activity. James is not against making plans; he is against the practical atheism of planning as though God were irrelevant and the future guaranteed. The phrase if the Lord wills is meant to reshape the heart's posture, not become a superstitious formula. Verse 17 broadens the point: sin is not only doing wrong but failing to do the good we know we ought to do.
basic.originalLanguages: The merchant plans to emporeuomai, to trade and profit. But life is an atmis, a mist or vapor, that vanishes. To plan without God is alazoneia, arrogant boasting, which James calls evil. The words move from confident commerce to the fragility of life to the pride that forgets its Maker.
basic.typology: The vanishing mist echoes the fleeting vapor of Ecclesiastes and the grass that withers in the Psalms and Isaiah, a theme fulfilled in the contrast with the eternal word and eternal life found in Christ. The call to live under God's will reflects the perfect submission of Jesus, who did only the Father's will and prayed not my will but yours.
basic.christ: Jesus lived the very posture James commands, always saying in effect if the Father wills, submitting even in Gethsemane, not my will but Yours be done. He is the eternal word that abides while our mist-like lives pass, and in Him our fleeting days are taken up into everlasting life. He also fulfilled all righteousness, never knowing the good and failing to do it, the sin verse 17 names.
basic.god: God is the sovereign Lord of every tomorrow, in whose will our living and doing are held. He is not an optional add-on to our plans but the One on whom our next breath depends. He is also the righteous Judge who counts as sin not only the evil we do but the good we leave undone. To live well is to live in humble reference to His will.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus told a parable of the rich fool who planned for years and died that night, Luke 12:16-21. Proverbs 27:1 says do not boast about tomorrow. Psalm 39:5 calls each life a mere breath. And Paul often qualified plans with if the Lord wills, 1 Corinthians 4:19.
basic.oneStory: Scripture keeps puncturing human pretension to control the future, from the rich fool to the withering grass, and keeps pointing to the God who holds all time and the Christ who submitted wholly to the Father's will. James applies this to everyday planning: our mist-like lives belong to the Lord, so we live saying if He wills, and we do the good we know. This humility is the wisdom from above at work, and it looks to the eternal life secured in Christ.

context.literary:
This short paragraph is the most compact piece of rhetoric in the letter, and it works by quoting its target. James lets the merchant speak first, in a single breath of confident planning: 'Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.' Every clause is a decision, every verb is a future, and God appears nowhere in the sentence. Verse 14 then interrupts the speech with a double blow, a statement and a question: you do not even know what tomorrow brings, and what is your life? The answer is a metaphor, a mist, and the verse closes on a pair of verbs that mirror each other, appearing and vanishing.

Verse 15 is the corrected speech. The same grammar of planning returns, but with the clause 'If the Lord is willing' placed at the front, and with two verbs under that condition, 'we will live and do'. James does not take planning away. He rewrites the sentence so that the first thing the merchant says is not 'we will go' but 'if the Lord wills'. Verse 16 then tells the reader what the first speech was: boasting, and verse 17 ends with a principle that stands almost as a proverb.

The opening words, 'Come now', in Greek are the same two words that open the warning to the rich in 5:1. They mark a rhetorical address, a summons to listen to a character, almost like a prophet calling a party to the bar. The two passages are therefore a matched pair, one addressing the merchants who plan and the other the landowners who hoard, and both are surrounded by the language of rich and proud. Between them stands the picture of wealth and time, which James has been developing from 1:9 to 11, where the rich man 'will fade away in the midst of his pursuits'.

Finally, notice what the paragraph does at the end of chapter 4. Having given a long call to repentance and a ban on judging, James ends on the plainest everyday example, a business plan. The shape of the chapter moves from desire to humility to time, and what holds them together is the question of who is king.
context.historical:
The Mediterranean world in which these Jewish believers lived was a network of trade. Roads, harbours and market towns linked cities across the empire, and diaspora Jews were well placed in that web, with kinsmen and synagogues in many ports. A merchant who planned to travel to a named city, stay a year and make a profit would not have struck anyone as unusual, and James is plainly not describing a villain. The picture is a respectable person making a rational plan. That is why the passage has bite.

Several features of ancient travel made the warning concrete. Voyages depended on seasons and winds, roads were dangerous, and sickness was common and often fatal. Life expectancy was short by modern standards and a year's plan was a bold act. The phrase 'you do not even know what will happen tomorrow' needed no argument for people who buried relatives often. The original audience also lived with the Old Testament proverb that said the same: 'Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring', Proverbs 27:1.

Speaking of the will of God had a settled place in the lives of the apostles. When Paul left Ephesus he said, 'I will come back to you if God is willing', Acts 18:21, and he wrote to Corinth, 'I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits', 1 Corinthians 16:7, and 'But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing', 1 Corinthians 4:19. Romans 1:10 puts it the same way. Hebrews 6:3 uses the same idea in 'if God permits'. The habit James recommends was already a mark of early Christian speech, and he is asking his readers to mean it.

The word 'boast' also had a social side. Merchants advertised themselves by their plans and their fortunes, and a culture driven by honour rewarded confident public speech. James takes that culture's most admired talk, the speech of the self made man, and puts a hand over its mouth. At the same time he does not attack trade or wealth creation as such. Lydia and Priscilla and Aquila worked at business and are praised in the New Testament, and the problem is the attitude.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs to a long biblical meditation on time and human frailty. The Old Testament uses the word hebel, breath or vapour, for the brevity of life: 'my days are but a breath', Job 7:16, 'Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath', Psalm 39:5, and the Preacher's refrain in Ecclesiastes. Psalm 90:5 and 6 compares people to grass that springs up in the morning and withers by evening, and Isaiah 40:6 to 8 sets the grass that withers against 'the word of our God' that 'stands forever'. Hosea 13:3 says rebels will be 'like the morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes'. James's mist belongs to this family.

The wisdom books supply the nearest teaching. 'A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps', Proverbs 16:9, and 'Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail', Proverbs 19:21. Neither text bans planning. Both put planning under God's purpose, which is exactly what James 4:15 does. Proverbs 27:1 gives the sharpest parallel and Ecclesiastes 6:12 asks 'Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?'

Jesus gives the New Testament counterpart in the parable of the rich fool, Luke 12:16 to 21. The farmer's plan to tear down barns and build bigger ones is wise as farming, and God calls him a fool because the plan did not include the night when 'your life will be required of you'. James seems to be writing within that teaching. Jesus also teaches in the Sermon on the Mount that disciples should not be anxious about tomorrow, Matthew 6:34, which is the other side of the same refusal to presume.

Paul's habit of saying 'if the Lord wills' shows how the church absorbed the teaching, and the way Acts reports Paul's changed plans shows it was lived. Verse 17 has echoes in Jesus' teaching that the servant who knows his master's will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows, Luke 12:47, and in Romans 14:23, 'everything that is not from faith is sin'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James wants to expose practical atheism without calling anyone an atheist. The merchants he describes would have said they believe in God. What he challenges is that their working life makes no reference to Him. The aim is to give his readers a question they can ask of any plan: where is God in this sentence?

He also intends to correct a false sense of control. People who have a calendar and a budget tend to feel that the future is manageable. The two questions in verse 14, one about tomorrow and one about the nature of life, are meant to break that illusion with something every reader knows is true. A mist has no say in how long it lasts. James is not trying to frighten his readers about death but to place their ambitions at their proper size.

The fix he proposes is small and very practical. He gives his readers a sentence to say and a habit of heart to go with it. The person who says 'if the Lord wills' in the right way has acknowledged that his life and his plans are borrowed. Such a person can plan with energy and without anxiety, because the future belongs to someone else and that someone is good.

Finally, verse 17 is placed where it is to prevent a different failure, the person who agrees with all of this and does nothing. James has taught throughout the letter that hearing without doing is self deception, and he closes the chapter by making that principle a rule: known good that is left undone is sin. His readers are meant to see that the humility he asks for is not an attitude only but a set of actions.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a mistaken attitude and prescribes a corrected one. Nothing in it forbids travel, trade, saving, budgeting or ambition. It does not even tell the merchant to stop making his plan, and it assumes that people will go on doing business. The prescription is the posture in verse 15, and the description of the merchant's speech is a negative example.

It is also not a formula. Saying 'if the Lord wills' at the end of every sentence can become a superstition, a verbal tic that adds nothing and may even hide a heart that still runs its own life. Paul's practice shows a living use: he said it where it was true to his actual dependence, and he also made plans, wrote them down and told people about them. The words matter because of the humility they express. Equally, a person who never says the words but lives openly in dependence on God has understood the passage better than the one who recites it.

Verse 17 is the most prescriptive line, but its scope needs care. It is not a licence for endless guilt about every good deed left undone, since no one can do every good thing. It speaks of a person who 'knows the right thing to do' and does not do it. The sin is the gap between conviction and action, and it applies to specific, known duties: a debt unpaid, a visit not made, a reconciliation avoided. It applies most naturally to anyone who has just heard the teaching of this very passage and does not act on it.

debates.question: Is James condemning planning itself?

views.label: No; he condemns godless presumption, not prudence
views.case: James does not forbid making plans or doing business, both assumed as normal. He condemns planning as though the future were guaranteed and God were irrelevant. The corrective, if the Lord wills, keeps planning under humble submission to God's sovereignty.

views.label: He targets the boastful spirit behind the plans
views.case: Others stress verse 16: the evil is boasting in proud intentions. The problem is the arrogant heart that credits itself with control, not the act of foresight. Wise, God-dependent planning is fully compatible with James.

debates.bearing: Both agree the sin is presumption, not prudence. Christians may and should plan, but always in conscious dependence on the Lord who holds tomorrow.

debates.question: What is the point of verse 17 on knowing good and not doing it?

views.label: It defines sins of omission
views.case: James broadens sin beyond wrongdoing to include failing to do the good we know we should. This is a sin of omission, and it presses home the whole letter's insistence that faith must act. Knowing the right and neglecting it is guilt, not neutrality.

views.label: It applies the planning lesson directly
views.case: Others read it as the immediate application: now that you know to live under God's will, failing to do so is sin. Either way it removes the excuse of ignorance and demands that knowledge become obedience.

debates.bearing: Whether taken broadly or as immediate application, the verse teaches that known good left undone is real sin, sealing the letter's call to be doers of the word.

study.originalLanguages:
The verse begins with age nun, 'Come now', a short imperative like a herald's call. It occurs in the New Testament only here and in James 5:1, where it summons the rich. In both places a group is called to account in the voice of a prophet.

The plan uses poreuo, to travel or go, in the future, 'we will go' (poreusometha). James used a related noun in 1:11, where the rich man 'will fade away in the midst of his pursuits' (poreiais), literally his journeys or ways of life. So 'we will travel' in 4:13 and 'in his travels he will fade' in 1:11 are linked: the merchant's journeys are the very path on which the mist disappears. 'Spend a year' is literally 'do a year', which treats time as a possession to be used, and 'make a profit' is kerdaino, the verb Jesus uses when He asks what a man gains if he 'gains the whole world', Matthew 16:26. Time itself is taken as a field to be mined.

The sentence in verse 14 'you do not even know what will happen tomorrow' is blunt, and the sense is not in doubt. The verb for knowing here is epistamai, to understand as a matter of fact, which makes the point that this ignorance is a plain fact and not a philosophical position.

The word 'mist' in verse 14 is atmis, a vapour or smoke. It occurs in the New Testament in Acts 2:19, in the quotation from Joel about 'vapor of smoke', and in Greek literature it describes steam or smoke from a fire. It is the word for a thing that is real but has no weight. The Hebrew equivalent in the background is hebel, 'breath', the word Job and the Preacher use, and Proverbs 21:6 applies it to wealth gained dishonestly, 'a vanishing mist'. The two participles that follow, phainomene and aphanizomene, 'appearing' and 'vanishing', are built on one root, the second a negation of the first, so the sentence can be heard as appears, disappears, with a pun in the Greek that English cannot keep.

Verse 15 begins anti tou legein hymas, 'instead of your saying', a construction which means the right speech replaces the wrong speech. The condition ean ho kyrios thelese is a conditional about God's will, and two verbs follow it, 'we shall live' and 'we shall do'. Grammatically both depend on the condition. That means it is not only the plan that is placed under the Lord's will but life itself. 'Lord' here may mean God the Father, but in the New Testament kyrios is regularly used of Jesus, and James has used it of Him in 1:1 and 2:1.

Verse 16 has alazoneia, in the plural, 'boastings' or 'pretensions'. Alazon in Greek was a stock figure, the braggart who claims more than he has, and the noun in 1 John 2:16 is 'the pride of life', the swagger of those who live as though their security were their own. The verb of boasting, kauchaomai, is used positively in the Bible when the boast is in the Lord, Jeremiah 9:23 and 24, and negatively here. The final word of the verse, ponera, 'evil', is blunt. Boasting is called evil without qualification.

Verse 17 uses kalon, the beautiful or good thing, a word for the noble act. The structure 'to the one who knows how to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin' puts the knowledge first and the omission last, so that the sin is located in the gap.

typology.type: The mist and the withering grass
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 40:6 to 8 and Psalm 90 picture human life as grass and breath against God's enduring word. James adds the mist. The pattern points beyond itself to the one who is the Word and who says 'before Abraham was born, I am', John 8:58, so that a mortal creature meets a life that does not vanish. Peter ties it together when he quotes Isaiah and adds 'this is the word that was preached to you', 1 Peter 1:24 and 25. The correspondence falls short as a comfort on its own, since a type of frailty cannot rescue anyone; the rescue is the resurrection of the one who is called the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

typology.type: The rich fool and his barns
typology.fulfillment: Jesus' parable in Luke 12:16 to 21 is the nearest narrative image to James's merchant. It uses the same shape of presumption, a plan for many years that ends in a single night. The type finds its fulfilment in Christ's own character, who was 'rich, yet for your sakes became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9, and who is the true heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2. Where the rich fool stored up for himself, Christ gave Himself. The parallel is only partial, because James's merchant is not called a fool and is given a way to put things right.

typology.type: Planning in submission to the Lord's will
typology.fulfillment: The pattern of acting 'if the Lord wills' is fulfilled in the Son who said 'not as I will, but as You will', Matthew 26:39, and 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me', John 4:34. Jesus planned, set His face toward Jerusalem, Luke 9:51, and told His disciples what would happen, yet every plan lay under the Father's will and was carried out by it. The type falls short in us because our submission is imperfect and often reluctant, while His was without flaw, and His obedience is what we lean on when ours fails.

typology.type: The traveller who does not know the road
typology.fulfillment: Abraham went out 'not knowing where he was going', Hebrews 11:8, and the pilgrim image runs through Israel's history, from Sinai to the exile. James's merchant knows his road and his destination and is therefore the opposite of Abraham. In Christ the pilgrim has a guide, who says 'I am the way', John 14:6, so that not knowing tomorrow need not mean not knowing where one is going. The correspondence is limited by the fact that the journey ends in a city 'whose architect and builder is God', Hebrews 11:10, which is a different destination from any merchant's.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by contrast with the plan it condemns. The merchant has no 'if the Lord is willing', and so his life runs on his own authority. The life of Jesus runs the other way. He says of Himself 'I have come down from heaven not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me', John 6:38, and in Gethsemane He puts that principle into words under the greatest strain: 'not as I will, but as You will', Matthew 26:39. If James's 'if the Lord is willing' is the sentence of a creature, the cross is that sentence spoken by the Son of God at the cost of everything.

It leads to Christ by the picture of time. The mist is a fair account of the human lot, and it is the truth about death. But Christ steps into the vapour, takes mortality upon Himself, and rises. Paul calls Him 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep', 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the writer to the Hebrews says that He holds 'the power of death', defeating it, Hebrews 2:14. The believer who plans under the will of God plans as one whose life is 'hidden with Christ in God', Colossians 3:3, a life that does not vanish with the mist. The effect of the resurrection on James's text is that the brevity of life becomes a reason for humility but not for despair.

The story of the rich fool at Luke 12 also leads to Him. The man was not 'rich toward God', and Christ is the one who shows what being rich toward God means: He who was rich became poor so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The merchant plans a profit; Christ pays for others, and His whole life is the transfer of wealth from the one who has everything to those who have nothing.

Verse 17 leads to Christ in a different way. If every person who knows what is right and fails to do it is guilty, then everyone is guilty, and the verse drives the reader towards the One who knew the right thing and did it every time. Paul says God made 'Him who knew no sin to be sin for us', 2 Corinthians 5:21. The sin of omission is covered by the obedience of the one who omitted nothing, and in that obedience the believer finds both pardon and the pattern of a life that finally turns knowledge into action, Titus 2:14.

There is also a link through the title 'Lord'. If the 'Lord' of verse 15 is Jesus, as Christians in the New Testament commonly meant, then James is asking his readers to place their plans under the lordship of the risen Christ, 'the Lord of both the dead and the living', Romans 14:9. We should be careful not to push the grammar further than James does, but the New Testament habit of speech makes the reading natural.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who holds time. James does not argue the point at length; he assumes it, and the whole logic of the paragraph depends on it: because tomorrow is known to the Lord and to no one else, every plan stands under His will. Proverbs 16:9 says 'a man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps', and Proverbs 19:21 says His purpose will prevail. This is the doctrine of providence at work in a business decision. It is not fatalism, since people plan and act, but it means the final word in every plan belongs to someone other than the planner.

It shows a God whose will is good enough to be trusted with the future. James's corrective, 'If the Lord is willing', is a sentence of peace, not resignation. The believer says it because the will in question belongs to the Father of lights who gives every good gift, James 1:17. If it were the will of an indifferent power, the sentence would be fatalistic; since it is the will of a generous Father, the sentence is a confession of confidence.

It shows God as the One who can be left out of our plans and is not removed by being left out. The merchants in verse 13 are not punished in the text, but they are called to account: boasting 'is evil'. God does not have to be invoked to be present, and His absence from a person's speech is noticed. This protects the doctrine of God's nearness from becoming a doctrine of convenience.

It shows God's relation to human frailty. The picture of a mist is not directed at God as an accusation. In Psalm 103 God 'knows how we are formed' and remembers that we are dust. The truth about life's brevity is the context for the greatness of His mercy and for the permanence of His word, Isaiah 40:8. The God who made mist-like creatures has not abandoned them to their own thinness.

It shows a God who takes omission seriously. Verse 17 teaches that God's moral concern is not satisfied by avoiding wrong, since He asks for the good that is known. Luke 12:47 and John 9:41 show the same view, that knowledge increases responsibility and that the one who sees clearly is the one who is accountable.

For worship the passage suggests that praise includes a way of holding the calendar. To thank God for the day, to commit a plan to Him in prayer, and to be ready to hear a different answer than the one hoped for is the form of worship James has in mind. The heart that prays 'if the Lord wills' in sincerity is already adoring, since it has said that God is God and the planner is not.

crossReferences.note: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. James's central point is already here, in almost the same words. It shows that his teaching is an application of Israel's own wisdom to merchants in the new covenant, and it explains why the word 'boast' appears twice in his argument.

The rich man plans bigger barns and years of ease, and God calls him a fool because that very night his life is required. It is the story behind James's warning, showing what planning without God looks like when it ends, and what it means to be rich toward God instead.

A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. It gives the exact balance of James 4:15: planning is allowed and expected, and the final direction belongs to the Lord. The verse also keeps James from being read as an argument against foresight.

You have made my days as handbreadths, and each man at his best exists as but a breath. The psalmist's confession of life's brevity is the same truth as the mist of verse 14, and it is said as prayer, which shows that the right response to frailty is to speak to God.

As Paul left Ephesus he said he would come back if God was willing. It shows the practice James teaches in an apostle's mouth, spoken naturally, and it shows that the phrase did not stop Paul from making plans and telling people about them.

Paul says he will come to Corinth shortly, if the Lord is willing. Here the condition is attached to a plan to confront arrogant people, so it appears in the heat of real ministry rather than only in gentle farewells, and it keeps boasting out of his own speech.

The rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits, like a flower in the scorching sun. This is the earlier image of the merchant's fate, and the shared word for journeys in the Greek makes the two passages a pair about wealth that passes.

The next paragraph also begins with 'Come now' and addresses people who have wealth, now as hoarders and oppressors. Read together they show James moving from the rich who plan as if they will live forever to the rich who hoard as if they will never be judged.

The servant who knows his master's will and does not follow it will be beaten with many blows. It supports the principle of James 4:17 that knowledge raises responsibility and that failing to do what is known is not neutral but culpable.

Everything that is not from faith is sin. Paul applies it to doubtful actions, and James applies a related principle to failed obedience. Both show that sin is not only breaking a command but acting, or failing to act, against what the heart knows.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story starts with creatures given time and told to use it. In Genesis 1 and 2 the man and woman are given work in the garden, and their days are good. Time is part of the gift. The fall brings the shadow: 'to dust you will return', Genesis 3:19, and from that point the Bible's talk of time is tinted by mortality, the breath that goes out and the grass that withers.

Part of the fall is the claim to control. The serpent offers the woman the chance to be 'like God', and the tower builders of Genesis 11 say 'let us make a name for ourselves'. Planning without God is the oldest project in human history, and James's merchants are heirs of Babel. Against that stands the call of Abraham, who is told to go without knowing where, and the whole history of Israel as a people who live by promise, not by plan, from the manna that could not be stored to the exile that took them away from every plan.

In Christ the story turns. He is the human being who lives in perfect dependence on the Father and who submits every plan to the Father's will, even when it leads to a cross. In His resurrection the mist is given a body that does not vanish. Because He lives, the brevity of life is not the last word, and the believer can plan with confidence and without arrogance. The Spirit given at Pentecost teaches the church to say 'if the Lord wills' not from fear but from trust, and the book of Acts shows the church making plans, changing them, and being led.

The story ends with a city where nothing is a mist. Revelation 21 and 22 describe a place without night, where God's servants 'will reign forever and ever', Revelation 22:5, and where there is no more death. The merchants of the earth who built their lives on trade lament the fall of Babylon in Revelation 18, and that lament is the last word about plans that left God out. Between the garden and the city, James's sentence is the believer's sentence: if the Lord wills, we will live, and do this or that.

quiz.q: What is wrong with the merchant's plan in verses 13 to 14?

options.text: He plans the future as if it were his to command, forgetting life is a fleeting mist.
options.note: Verses 13 to 14: the sin is presumption about a future only God holds.

options.text: He assumes he will live and profit though he cannot know tomorrow.
options.note: True to the text, describing the false certainty involved.

options.text: He is doing business at all, which James forbids.
options.note: James does not forbid commerce; he rebukes godless self-assurance.

options.text: He is too cautious and should take bigger risks.
options.note: The problem is arrogance, not caution.

quiz.q: How does James say we ought to speak about our plans?

options.text: If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.
options.note: Verse 15: plans held humbly under God's sovereign will.

options.text: With humble dependence on God rather than proud self-assurance.
options.note: True to the heart of it, if less exact than the words given.

options.text: By making no plans at all and simply waiting.
options.note: James corrects the attitude, not the act of planning.

options.text: By confidently asserting our goals to guarantee success.
options.note: That is the boasting James calls evil.

quiz.q: What image does James use for human life in verse 14?

options.text: A mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
options.note: Verse 14: life is brief and fragile, like a vapor.

options.text: Something brief and fragile, here and quickly gone.
options.note: True to the sense, capturing the mist image in other words.

options.text: A solid structure we can build on for decades.
options.note: The opposite of the fleeting mist James describes.

options.text: An endless span we can plan without limit.
options.note: James stresses precisely that our time is short and uncertain.

quiz.q: What does James call boasting in one's own plans?

options.text: Arrogant boasting, which he says is evil.
options.note: Verse 16: all such proud self-confidence is evil.

options.text: Proud presumption that leaves God out of the future.
options.note: True to why it is evil, naming the underlying pride.

options.text: A harmless and even admirable confidence.
options.note: James judges it evil, not admirable.

options.text: The proper attitude for ambitious believers.
options.note: The opposite of what James commends.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 teach about sin?

options.text: Knowing the right thing to do and failing to do it is sin.
options.note: Verse 17: sins of omission are real guilt, not neutrality.

options.text: Sin includes neglecting the good we know we ought to do.
options.note: True restatement of the principle of omission.

options.text: Only actively doing wrong counts as sin.
options.note: James expands sin to include known good left undone.

options.text: Ignorance and neglect are always excusable.
options.note: The verse removes the excuse when the good is known.

questions: James pictures confident plans made without reference to God. Where do your own plans quietly assume you are in control of the future?
Your life is a mist. How does honestly facing the brevity of life change what you give your days to?
What would it look like, practically, to hold your plans this week with a genuine if the Lord wills rather than as a superstitious phrase?
Verse 17 says known good left undone is sin. Is there a good you clearly know you should do but keep postponing?
Jesus prayed not my will but Yours. In what decision right now do you most need to pray that same prayer?

translationNotes.note: Carry on business renders emporeuomai, to travel and trade for profit; the picture is an ordinary merchant venture, rebuked not for commerce but for godless presumption.
Mist renders atmis, a vapor or puff of steam, echoing the fleeting breath of the Psalms and the vapor of Ecclesiastes.
Proud intentions renders alazoneia, arrogant boasting; James judges all such self-confident bragging about the future to be evil.
